```{r setup}
library(betwixt)
```

## Why an intermediate vocabulary?

Betwixt operates between candidate knowledge and its subsequent representation in tabular, graph, or tensor form. Its intermediate vocabulary preserves semantic identity and review state without requiring commitment to a particular domain ontology or output representation.

At the time of review, the components of an assertion may not yet have mappings to external vocabularies. However, subjects must be deterministically identifiable, either through an absolute IRI or a declared identifier resolution rule.

For example, a reviewed assertion might consist of:

``` text
subject:   Q223
predicate: depicts
value:     cardigan
```

The subject `Q223` may be a local identifier that resolves deterministically to an absolute IRI. The predicate `depicts` may identify a property defined within the Betwixt table, while `cardigan` may remain a literal value or subsequently be mapped to a controlled concept.

Betwixt does not require external ontology mappings before review. It requires sufficient semantic identification to preserve the meaning of assertions across subsequent transformations.

The Betwixt vocabulary represents *semantic assertions independently of their eventual data representation or domain ontology*. It is deliberately small: its purpose is to preserve assertion structure, semantic identity, review state, and the information required for reproducible transformations.

A reviewed Betwixt table may be retained as a typed tabular dataset, projected into an RDF knowledge graph, or transformed into a tensor. None of these representations is privileged as the underlying semantic model.

## Assertions

The central class is `btx:Assertion`. Its subject, predicate, and value are represented lexically, allowing assertions to remain independent of a particular output format (f.e., graph, table, or tensor.)

``` turtle
btx:Assertion
    a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "Assertion" ;
    rdfs:comment "An intermediate semantic assertion represented independently of a domain ontology." .

btx:subject
    a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain btx:Assertion ;
    rdfs:range xsd:string ;
    rdfs:label "subject" ;
    rdfs:comment
        "The lexical representation of the subject of an assertion.
        The value MUST be deterministically resolvable to an absolute
        IRI, either directly or through a declared identifier 
        resolution rule. This preserves subject identity independently 
        of subsequent tabular, graph, or tensor projections." .

btx:predicate
    a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain btx:Assertion ;
    rdfs:range xsd:string ;
    rdfs:label "predicate" ;
    rdfs:comment "The lexical representation of the predicate of an assertion." .

btx:value
    a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain btx:Assertion ;
    rdfs:range xsd:string ;
    rdfs:label "value" ;
    rdfs:comment "The lexical representation of the value of an assertion." .
```

The subject must be deterministically resolvable to an absolute IRI. The predicate identifies the semantic relationship represented by the assertion, normally corresponding to a semantically defined column in its containing table. The value may represent a literal or a resource identifier, with its intended interpretation and datatype preserved through the table schema or associated metadata.

The lexical representation does not imply that all values are semantically strings. It separates the storage of assertion components from their interpretation in subsequent projections.

Using datatype properties here is intentional. Betwixt records the lexical components of assertions without requiring their immediate interpretation as RDF resources or typed RDF literals.

A subject may be represented by a local inventory number, Wikibase QID, or absolute IRI, provided its identity can be resolved deterministically. Predicates may be defined within the table's own namespace, and values may remain literals or be mapped to identified resources.

The vocabulary therefore preserves semantic commitments without requiring a graph representation. RDF resource identification and literal typing are applied when appropriate during projection.

A concrete assertion can consequently be represented as:

``` turtle
:assertion-5
    a btx:Assertion ;
    btx:subject "Q223" ;
    btx:predicate "depicts" ;
    btx:value "cardigan" ;
    btx:status btx:Deferred .
```

This is valid RDF, but it does **not** assert the domain triple `Q223 depicts cardigan`. Instead, it describes an intermediate assertion whose semantic components can subsequently be resolved and projected.

`btx:assertion` associates assertions with a containing resource, while `btx:rowId` and `btx:assertionId` identify their table-scoped row and assertion coordinates, respectively.

## Tables and coordinates

`btx:Table` represents an identified collection of rows and semantically classified columns, maintained according to tidy-data principles. A table is the semantic unit within which Betwixt organizes assertions and their coordinates.

```
btx:Table
    a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "Table"@en ;
    rdfs:comment
        "An identified collection of rows and
        semantically classified columns, maintained
        according to tidy-data principles and supporting
        stable semantic assertions and multiple data
        projections."@en 
        
btx:rowId
    a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain btx:Assertion ;
    rdfs:range xsd:integer ;
    rdfs:label "row identifier" ;
    rdfs:comment
        "The integer coordinate identifying the source
        row of an assertion within its containing
        Betwixt table. Row identifiers are scoped to a
        table; transformations producing a new table
        establish new coordinates, while source
        coordinates may be retained as provenance." .

btx:assertionId
    a owl:DatatypeProperty ;
    rdfs:domain btx:Assertion ;
    rdfs:range xsd:integer ;
    rdfs:label "assertion identifier" ;
    rdfs:comment
        "The integer coordinate identifying an assertion
        within a Betwixt table. Assertion identifiers
        are unique within their containing table. A
        transformation producing a new table establishes
        new assertion coordinates." .
```
Each table has a stable IRI (`table_iri`) and may have a human-readable local identifier (`table_id`). The table IRI establishes the identification context for its rows and locally defined predicates.

For example:

```         
@prefix tbl: <https://example.org/museum-objects#> .

<https://example.org/museum-objects>
    a btx:Table ;
    rdfs:label "museum_objects"@en ;
    btx:assertion tbl:assertion_1 .

tbl:assertion_1
    a btx:Assertion ;
    btx:rowId 1 ;
    btx:assertionId 1 ;
    btx:subject "Q101" ;
    btx:predicate "height_cm" ;
    btx:value "120" ;
    btx:status btx:Corroborated .
```

In this example, `Q101` is assumed to resolve through a declared identifier rule, and `height_cm` identifies a predicate defined within the table's semantic context.

`btx:rowId` identifies the source row of an assertion, while `btx:assertionId` identifies the individual assertion. Both coordinates are integers scoped to their containing table.

When two tables are joined or bound into a new identified table, the resulting table receives its own IRI and coordinate system. Original row identifiers may be retained as provenance, together with the identities of their source tables.

The coordinates of an assertion must therefore be interpreted together with its containing table. They are not global identifiers.

### Column definitions and datatypes

Betwixt does not require separate `btx:Row` or `btx:Column` classes. Rows are represented through table-scoped coordinates, while column semantics are maintained through table conventions, predicate identities, and schema metadata.

Each reviewable column represents a semantic predicate. Its values may have a native datatype in the tabular representation, such as integer, numeric, logical, or character.

For example, an R integer column:

```         
height_cm = c(120L, 145L, 180L)
```

may be represented lexically in Betwixt assertions while retaining its datatype through the table schema.

An RDF graph projection can then produce:

```         
<https://example.org/Q101>     
    tbl:height_cm "120"^^xsd:integer .
```

The typed literal is derived from the declared column semantics, not inferred merely from the lexical value `"120"`.

A tabular projection can preserve the integer column directly. A tensor projection can use an appropriate numerical representation.

This approach separates semantic typing from the particular mechanisms used to store or exchange values. It also requires that datatype information remain available through the table schema or associated metadata whenever assertions are exported independently of their original table.

Betwixt does not need to reproduce an entire tabular schema vocabulary. Existing mechanisms, including native R types, CSVW metadata, and RDF datatype declarations, can provide the required typing information.

## Review state

Review state is represented separately from the content of an assertion.

``` turtle
...
```

`btx:Corroborated` means that the candidate assertion survived review unchanged. `btx:Corrected` records that the reviewed value differs from the candidate. `btx:Rejected` records rejection, while `btx:Deferred` explicitly preserves an unresolved decision. `btx:Pending` represents an assertion whose review has not yet been finalised.

This distinction matters because the result of review is not merely another table of values. Betwixt also preserves **what happened to the proposed knowledge during review**.

## From review matrices to assertions

A Betwixt review is naturally represented in wide form during human review. Candidate values, reviewed values, and review states occupy corresponding coordinates.

`project_review_long()` transforms the reviewed matrix into atomic assertions:

```{r}
path <- system.file(
  "examples",
  "muis-garments-review_1-finalised.html",
  package = "betwixt"
)
review <- read_review(path)
long <- project_review_long(review)
head(long)
```

Each row in the long projection represents one assertion. row_id identifies the source row within the containing Betwixt table, while assertion_number provides the assertion coordinate in the canonical projection.

These correspond conceptually to `btx:rowId` and `btx:assertionId` in the vocabulary.

The coordinates are scoped to the identified table. When a transformation creates a new Betwixt table, new coordinates are established, while source table identities and coordinates may be preserved as provenance.

The long projection provides an assertion-oriented representation of the reviewed table. It can support subsequent tabular, RDF graph, or tensor projections without making any one of these the required final representation.

This transformation provides the bridge between a human-oriented review matrix and the assertion-oriented representation used by the Betwixt RDF vocabulary.

## Mappings

Keeping assertions lexical allows semantic resolution to happen separately from review. A `btx:Mapping` records a correspondence between a lexical Betwixt term and a target RDF resource.

Mappings can apply to any of the three structural positions of an assertion:

``` turtle
btx:AssertionRole
    a owl:Class ;
    rdfs:label "Assertion role" .

btx:Subject a btx:AssertionRole .
btx:Predicate a btx:AssertionRole .
btx:Value a btx:AssertionRole .
```

For example:

``` turtle
:mapping-1
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "depicts" ;
    btx:target wdt:P121 ;
    btx:role btx:Predicate .
```

The mapping does not state that the lexical term `"depicts"` is universally equivalent to `wdt:P121`. It records a correspondence that may warrant that transformation in an appropriate context.

This distinction is deliberate: **Betwixt does not align ontologies. It records reviewed correspondences that can warrant bounded semantic projections.**

## Bounded semantic projection

Consider a reviewed assertion:

``` turtle
:assertion-5
    a btx:Assertion ;
    btx:subject "Q223" ;
    btx:predicate "depicts" ;
    btx:value "Q456" ;
    btx:status btx:Corroborated .
```

Together with reviewed mappings for its three components, this may warrant a projection such as:

``` turtle
wd:Q223 wdt:P121 wd:Q456 .
```

The projected triple belongs to the target semantic environment. The Betwixt assertion remains the representation-independent intermediate statement from which the projection was derived.

RDF graph projection is one possible use of Betwixt. The same reviewed assertions may also support typed tabular datasets or tensor representations, subject to the semantics and constraints of those formats.

Betwixt does not attempt to replace Wikibase, Schema.org, CIDOC CRM, RiC-O, or another domain model. It preserves semantic assertions and reviewed correspondences sufficiently explicitly that transformations into these environments can be reproducible and auditable.

In this sense, Betwixt sits literally *betwixt* documentary or computational evidence and its subsequent semantic representations:

**candidate knowledge → human review → stabilised assertions → reproducible semantic projections**

These projections may produce typed tables, RDF graphs, or tensors. Where a projection crosses independently governed semantic environments, Betwixt supports bounded correspondence through explicit, reviewable mappings.

## From mappings to federation

The need for mappings becomes particularly clear when knowledge is exchanged between independently governed knowledge graphs.

Two graphs may describe the same person, use apparently equivalent predicates, and classify that person using apparently equivalent concepts, while sharing none of the identifiers involved. Neither graph is necessarily wrong, incomplete, or subordinate to the other. They simply operate within different semantic environments.

This is a normal situation in a federation.

Consider the Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space (FUDSS) and Wikidata. Both can express the proposition:

> **Béla Bartók — instance of — human**

In FUDSS:

``` turtle
fudss:Q5613 fudsst:P14 fudss:Q6 .
```

In Wikidata:

``` turtle
wd:Q83326 wdt:P31 wd:Q5 .
```

The propositions are readily recognisable to a human as corresponding. Computationally, however, every component is different.

| Role      | FUDSS         | Wikidata    |
|-----------|---------------|-------------|
| subject   | `fudss:Q5613` | `wd:Q83326` |
| predicate | `fudsst:P14`  | `wdt:P31`   |
| value     | `fudss:Q6`    | `wd:Q5`     |

Nothing in the RDF statements themselves establishes these correspondences.

A federation therefore needs more than access to both graphs. It needs an explicit account of **which semantic correspondences are sufficiently warranted for a particular exchange**.

This is where Betwixt enters the federation.

## Candidate correspondences

Rather than immediately asserting global equivalence between the resources, Betwixt can represent the proposed correspondences as candidates.

For the Bartók assertion, three correspondences are required:

``` text
subject:    fudss:Q5613  →  wd:Q83326
predicate:  fudsst:P14   →  wdt:P31
value:      fudss:Q6     →  wd:Q5
```

These are not merely technical lookup rules. Each is a semantic claim.

The subject correspondence claims that the two identifiers refer appropriately to Béla Bartók for the intended projection. The predicate correspondence claims that the two properties can play corresponding roles. The value correspondence claims that the two resources provide compatible classifications for the purpose at hand.

Betwixt therefore treats mappings as material that can itself be reviewed.

## Reviewing the correspondence

The same candidate-review workflow used for ordinary semantic assertions can be used for proposed mappings.

For example:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
mapping <- create_candidate_dataset(
  label = "FUDSS instance of → Wikidata instance of",
  subject = "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/P14"
) |>
  add_candidate_column(
    name = "predicate",
    value = "https://usebetwixt.com/ns/target"
  ) |>
  add_candidate_column(
    name = "value",
    value = "http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/P31"
  )
```

The proposed correspondence can now be corroborated, corrected, rejected, or deferred.

This is important because mappings are not necessarily permanent or universal. A correspondence that is adequate for one research question, data exchange, or federation may be too broad for another.

## From reviewed correspondence to projection

Once the relevant correspondences have been reviewed, Betwixt can represent them explicitly:

``` turtle
:mapping-subject
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q5613" ;
    btx:target wd:Q83326 ;
    btx:role btx:Subject .

:mapping-predicate
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/P14" ;
    btx:target wdt:P31 ;
    btx:role btx:Predicate .

:mapping-value
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q6" ;
    btx:target wd:Q5 ;
    btx:role btx:Value .
```

Together with the reviewed source assertion, these correspondences provide the warrant for the bounded projection:

``` turtle
wd:Q83326 wdt:P31 wd:Q5 .
```

The important point is what has **not** happened.

FUDSS has not adopted Wikidata's ontology. Wikidata has not adopted the FUDSS ontology. Neither graph has surrendered its identifiers or governance. Betwixt has not asserted global `owl:sameAs` or `owl:equivalentProperty` relationships.

Instead, the federation has established enough reviewed semantic correspondence to perform a declared projection.

## Why this matters for bounded federation

This changes the interoperability problem.

A federation does not necessarily need complete ontology alignment before independently governed graphs can exchange knowledge. It needs sufficient correspondence for the particular inference or exchange being attempted.

Betwixt makes that correspondence an explicit object of knowledge production:

**local assertion → candidate correspondence → human review → warranted projection**

The boundary is therefore not merely technical. It records the limits within which a semantic transformation is considered justified.

This is what makes the projection **bounded**.

A mapping can be useful without claiming universal equivalence. A local vocabulary can remain local. A specialised knowledge graph can preserve distinctions that do not exist in Wikidata while still projecting those assertions for which an adequate correspondence has been established.

Conversely, when no satisfactory correspondence exists, the correct outcome can be `deferred` rather than forcing an alignment.

The purpose of Betwixt is therefore not to eliminate semantic difference between federated graphs. It is to make the decisions required to cross those differences **explicit, reviewable, reproducible and revisable**.

``` turtle
@prefix btx: <https://usebetwixt.com/ns/> .
@prefix wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> .
@prefix wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/> .
@prefix fudss: <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/> .
@prefix fudsst: <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .

# Betwixt vocabulary ----------------------------------------------------------

<https://usebetwixt.com/ns/betwixt.ttl>
    a <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#Ontology> .

# Source assertion ------------------------------------------------------------

# FUDSS:
# Béla Bartók — instance of — human
#
# fudss:Q5613 fudsst:P14 fudss:Q6 .

<https://usebetwixt.com/examples/bartok/assertion/1>
    a btx:Assertion ;
    btx:subject "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q5613" ;
    btx:predicate "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/P14" ;
    btx:value "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q6" ;
    btx:status btx:Corroborated .

# Subject mapping -------------------------------------------------------------

<https://usebetwixt.com/examples/bartok/mapping/subject>
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q5613" ;
    btx:target wd:Q83326 ;
    btx:role btx:Subject .

# Predicate mapping -----------------------------------------------------------

<https://usebetwixt.com/examples/bartok/mapping/predicate>
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/P14" ;
    btx:target wdt:P31 ;
    btx:role btx:Predicate .

# Value mapping ---------------------------------------------------------------

<https://usebetwixt.com/examples/bartok/mapping/value>
    a btx:Mapping ;
    btx:source "https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/Q6" ;
    btx:target wd:Q5 ;
    btx:role btx:Value .

# Bounded semantic projection -------------------------------------------------

# Wikidata:
# Béla Bartók — instance of — human

wd:Q83326 wdt:P31 wd:Q5 .
```
